cim: Seventy Systematic Reviews Reveal Artificial Intelligence in Diabetes Faces Implementation Barriers
cim_eredeti: Seventy Systematic Reviews Reveal Artificial Intelligence in Diabetes Faces Implementation Barriers
szoveg_eredeti:
Seventy Systematic Reviews Reveal Artificial Intelligence in Diabetes Faces Implementation Barriers

A comprehensive tertiary review examining 70 systematic reviews of artificial intelligence in diabetes mellitus reveals that while computational research has accelerated rapidly, the overall evidence base remains clinically fragmented and heavily skewed toward specific disease subtypes and modalities. Led by Sander M. W. Janssen and colleagues, the synthesis evaluates secondary studies published between 2014 and October 2025 across multiple clinical domains. Rather than demonstrating immediate translational readiness, the secondary literature indicates that AI development is at a transitional stage characterized by uneven methodological rigor and significant barriers to routine clinical deployment. Across the analyzed literature, researchers identified sharp disparities between technically mature experimental algorithms and their practical integration into real-world healthcare settings. By examining reviews spanning type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes, as well as critical complications, the investigation offers the first high-level systematic overview assessing the structural maturity and reliability of artificial intelligence across the entire diabetes continuum.

The urgency surrounding computational tools stems from the immense and expanding global burden of diabetes mellitus and its complex multi-system complications. Source data indicate that diabetes prevalence reached approximately 9.3 percent of the global population in 2019, with projections indicating an increase to 10.2 percent, amounting to 578 million individuals, by 2030 and 10.9 percent, or 700 million people, by 2045. More recent estimates from the Global Burden of Disease Study documented 529 million affected individuals in 2021, with numbers anticipated to escalate to 1.31 billion by 2050. The condition manifests predominantly as type 2 diabetes, which represents more than 90 percent of all cases and had an estimated adult prevalence of 10.5 percent in 2021. Meanwhile, autoimmune type 1 diabetes affects roughly 9 million people worldwide, including more than 1.5 million children, and gestational diabetes complicates an estimated 14 percent of pregnancies globally. Managing these conditions requires continuous monitoring, personalized behavioral strategies, and timely interventions to avert severe microvascular and macrovascular sequelae.

The clinical burden of diabetes is compounded by debilitating complications that provide distinct targets for automated diagnostic and predictive technologies. Diabetic kidney disease, also termed diabetic nephropathy, affects up to 40 percent of individuals with diabetes and represents the foremost cause of chronic kidney failure globally, progressing through metabolic, hemodynamic, and inflammatory pathways that frequently remain clinically silent until advanced organ damage occurs. Diabetic foot ulcers present another severe manifestation, exhibiting a worldwide prevalence of 6.3 percent among individuals with diabetes; between 50 and 60 percent of these ulcerations progress to active infections, 15 percent lead to lower-limb amputations, and patients face a five-year mortality rate 2.5 times higher than those without ulcers. In parallel, diabetic retinopathy constitutes the leading cause of preventable adult blindness, with an estimated 22 percent prevalence affecting approximately 103 million people in 2020 and projected to reach 160 million by 2045. These disparate pathologies generate unique diagnostic imaging, physiological sensor feeds, and clinical records that demand targeted computational approaches.

To rigorously evaluate the existing secondary evidence base, the investigators implemented a tertiary review protocol based on guidelines formulated by Kitchenham and Charters for software engineering and adapted from medical syntheses. The study executed comprehensive multi-database queries across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Explore covering literature published from January 1, 2014, through October 31, 2025. An initial retrieval yielded 912 citations, which narrowed to 595 records following the removal of duplicate entries across platforms. Title and abstract screening subsequently identified 155 candidate publications for full-text eligibility appraisal against explicit inclusion criteria. A total of 63 studies were excluded during this stage, consisting of 44 papers that lacked systematic methodology, 14 that did not align with specific clinical research questions, and five non-journal items. The remaining 92 secondary reviews underwent formal quality assessment using the four-item DARE criteria established by York University Centre for Reviews and Dissemination, with 22 low-scoring studies eliminated.

The final curated corpus comprised 70 rigorous secondary studies, encompassing 60 systematic reviews and 10 formal meta-analyses distributed across prominent international biomedical publications. The Journal of Medical Internet Research hosted five of these reviews, followed by Artificial Intelligence in Medicine with four, though most contributing journals published only one or two eligible syntheses. Geographically, institutional affiliations were concentrated in the United Kingdom with 13 publications, the United States with 10, and China with nine, collectively accounting for 32 of the 70 included works. Publication trends revealed a pronounced acceleration after 2020, reaching an annual peak of 16 secondary reviews in 2025 alone. Across all 70 syntheses, the authors recovered complete inclusion lists representing 2,382 citations and 1,988 unique primary investigations, with only 292 primary studies appearing in multiple reviews. Corrected covered area analysis demonstrated a slight overall overlap of 0.29 percent, confirming that the analyzed secondary literature generally drew from distinct primary research pools.

Mapping the distribution of computational research revealed substantial structural imbalances across clinical categories, with primary attention centered on type 2 diabetes across 50 reviews, closely followed by type 1 diabetes. In contrast, gestational diabetes and diabetic kidney disease remained the least researched clinical categories in the synthesized corpus. A co-occurrence network analysis of titles and abstracts delineated five primary interconnected research domains: clinical and behavioral evaluations assessing digital tools like chatbots and lifestyle interventions against biomarkers such as glycated hemoglobin; supervised learning and predictive modeling using traditional algorithms; decision-support and continuous monitoring utilizing deep learning and continuous glucose monitor streams; precision and reliability studies focusing on false positives, sensitivity limits, hypoglycemia, and neuropathy; and systemic integration examining interpretability and data governance. Dense conceptual clustering showed that these domains evolve simultaneously, yet their close interaction highlights how clinical utility remains contingent on addressing technical and methodological vulnerabilities.

Detailed examination of analytical pipelines revealed distinct pairings between data modalities and machine learning paradigms across different clinical challenges. Tabular datasets extracted from electronic medical records and registries heavily dominated research, appearing in 31 type 2 diabetes reviews and 21 type 1 diabetes reviews. Conversely, image-based inputs were concentrated in diabetic foot ulcer screening across 12 reviews and diabetic retinopathy across 10 reviews, where automated computer vision algorithms were predominantly deployed. Wearables and continuous glucose monitoring data featured primarily in type 1 diabetes across 14 reviews and type 2 diabetes across 17 reviews, feeding predictive time-series models and clinical decision-support architectures for insulin titration.
